text: If your organization has no SRE practice today, there's no shared vocabulary for it and no track record of it working here. Announcing a company-wide SRE initiative into that vacuum reads as more process with no proof it pays off, and meets exactly the resistance you'd expect. Google's SRE book is clear that SRE is a set of practices solving a real operational problem, not a certification rolled out top down. Organizations that succeed start with a pilot — one service, one team, a defined trial period.

Not every service makes a good pilot. The right one has three properties: it's important enough that improving its reliability visibly matters, it's owned by one willing team, and its operational pain is real and already acknowledged — frequent pages, a recent bad incident, inconsistent on-call. A service nobody cares about proves nothing even if the pilot goes well, because no one was watching. A service that's both critical and already hurting is where a measurable improvement gets noticed.

The pilot's actual content is defining a Service Level Objective with the team that owns the service, deriving an error budget from it, and running the team's real work against that budget for one full measurement period, usually a quarter. This is where the pilot becomes real instead of staying theoretical. An SLO nobody uses to make an actual decision, like pausing a risky deploy, is a document, not a practice. The point is proving the error budget changes what a team does.

At the end of the pilot, the case for expanding SRE practice has to rest on the team's own before-and-after numbers — incident frequency, time to detect and resolve, how many times the error budget genuinely changed a decision — and on how the team describes the experience. A pilot that improved a metric but made the team miserable is not a story anyone else will volunteer for. A pilot that improved the metric and that the team would recommend to a peer is the real proof, turning the next team's adoption into a request instead of a mandate.

That's the whole model for introducing SRE where it doesn't exist yet: one well-chosen pilot service, a real SLO and error budget actually used to make decisions, and evidence strong enough that the next team asks for it. Next lesson looks at what that error budget is really doing once it's in place — the genuine tension between reliability work and feature velocity, and why the error budget is the real mechanism for negotiating that tradeoff instead of ignoring it.
